concept.name: Metrics Cardinality Control

relationships.description: Connects Metrics Cardinality Control to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Metrics cardinality is the number of unique label-value combinations (`metric_name + {k=v}`) tracked in a Time-Series Database; unbounded labels like `user_id` or `request_id` explode inverted indexes, exhausting TSDB RAM and crashing Prometheus/Mimir.
spark.keyTakeaway: Never put high-cardinality identifiers (user IDs, IPs, URLs with UUIDs, pod hashes) into metric labels; keep active series bounded by dropping/normalizing labels at scrape time and use Logs or Trace Exemplars for per-request debugging.

concept.whyItMatters: In Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, and Mimir, every unique combination of metric name and label values creates a separate time series with its own in-memory Head chunk, inverted index entry, and 2-hour block compaction cost. A single developer adding `user_id` or raw `http_path` to a counter or 12-bucket histogram can turn 500 series into 50 million series overnight—consuming 150+ GB of RAM, stalling compaction, and spiking Datadog/cloud monitoring bills by 10x.
whenToUse: Instrumenting multi-tenant or high-traffic microservices with Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, or Datadog where metrics aggregate across thousands of pods and endpoints.
Enforcing guardrails at the OTel Collector or Prometheus scrape/remote-write layer before untrusted application metrics hit central TSDB storage.
Designing histograms and SLOs (`http_request_duration_seconds`) where multiplying `N` labels by 12–15 `le` buckets rapidly multiplies total series count.
whenNotToUse: When you genuinely need per-user, per-request, or per-IP debugging—use structured logs (Loki/ClickHouse), distributed traces (Tempo/Jaeger), or Exemplars instead of metrics.
Analytics/BI pipelines (BigQuery, ClickHouse, Snowflake) designed for high-cardinality `GROUP BY user_id` queries rather than 15-second TSDB scrape intervals.
Tiny single-node deployments (<10k total series) where aggressive label-dropping rules add operational complexity without meaningful memory savings.
keyPoints: Total cardinality is the Cartesian product of active label values: `50 endpoints × 5 status_codes × 4 methods × 100 pods × 12 histogram buckets = 1,200,000 series` from one metric.
In Prometheus, each active series consumes roughly 3–5 KB of RAM in the Head block; 10 million active series requires ~30–50 GB of RAM before any query runs.
Normalize dynamic URLs (`/users/98421/orders` -> `/users/:id/orders`) inside the HTTP router middleware *before* incrementing Prometheus/OTel counters.
Use OpenTelemetry `attributesprocessor` or Prometheus `metric_relabel_configs` (`labeldrop`, `drop`, `keep`) to strip runaway labels at ingestion.
Exemplars attach a `trace_id` to a histogram bucket sample without creating a new time series, giving you one-click drilldown from a p99 latency spike to the exact user/request trace.

examples.title: Unnormalized REST Paths OOM-Kill Production Prometheus
examples.scenario: A new Spring Boot microservice exposed `http_server_requests_seconds` using the raw request URI (`/api/v1/invoices/inv_88219a`) instead of the matched route template. Within 4 hours, active series jumped from 180k to 14.2M.
examples.outcome: Prometheus OOM-killed repeatedly during 2-hour head-block compaction. Adding a `metric_relabel_configs` rule to drop `uri` values not matching known patterns restored stability, followed by configuring Spring Boot's `WebMvcTagsProvider` to emit parameterized route templates.

examples.title: Histogram Bucket Multiplication in Kubernetes Ingress
examples.scenario: An NGINX Ingress controller exported a 16-bucket latency histogram labeled by `exported_namespace`, `ingress`, `service`, `status`, and `pod` across 400 pods, generating 8.5M series and $18k/month in SaaS custom-metric overages.
examples.outcome: Replacing fixed-bucket histograms with Prometheus Native Histograms (exponential buckets stored in a single series) and dropping `pod` from ingress-level metrics reduced series count by 94% (to 510k) while improving p99 accuracy.

tradeOffs.factor: Coarse Metric Labels vs. Granular Per-Pod / Per-Tenant Labels
tradeOffs.pro: Dropping `pod` or `tenant_id` from high-frequency histograms slashes TSDB RAM and query latency by 10–100x.
tradeOffs.con: You lose the ability to slice a p99 latency spike by a specific noisy neighbor tenant or faulty pod directly in Grafana.

tradeOffs.pro: Collector/Prometheus relabeling acts as a central circuit breaker that protects the TSDB even when a team deploys a buggy metric.
tradeOffs.con: Dropping a label via `labeldrop` without pre-aggregating creates duplicate timestamp collisions (`out of order` / `duplicate sample` errors) unless you use `metricstransform` aggregation.

tradeOffs.factor: Native Histograms vs. Classic `le` Bucket Histograms
tradeOffs.pro: Native (exponential) histograms store all buckets inside a single time series, cutting histogram cardinality by 10–20x while eliminating manual bucket tuning.
tradeOffs.con: Requires Prometheus >= 2.40+ / OTel Collector support and PromQL `histogram_quantile()` syntax adjustments across existing dashboards.

failureModes.name: Head-Block OOM & Compaction Stall
failureModes.description: Rapidly churning ephemeral labels (e.g., `pod_name` or `job_id` in short-lived CronJobs) fill the Prometheus 2-hour Head block with millions of dead series; compaction exceeds memory limits and crashes in a loop.
failureModes.mitigation: Set `sample_limit: 50000` and `label_limit: 30` per scrape job so rogue targets fail to scrape rather than crashing the central TSDB.

failureModes.name: Duplicate Sample Collisions After `labeldrop`
failureModes.description: Using `labeldrop` in Prometheus to strip `instance` or `user_id` leaves multiple distinct series with identical remaining labels; Prometheus rejects the colliding timestamps and drops data.
failureModes.mitigation: Drop the entire offending metric (`action: drop`) at scrape time or aggregate it properly using OTel Collector `metricstransform` / recording rules before storage.

failureModes.name: Inverted Index Query Timeout
failureModes.description: Queries like `sum by (route) (rate(http_requests_total{env="prod"}[5m]))` must intersect postings lists across millions of series, causing 30s+ query timeouts and Grafana 504s.
failureModes.mitigation: Pre-aggregate high-fanout metrics using Prometheus Recording Rules (`job:http_requests:rate5m`) and limit regex matchers (`=~ ".*"`) on high-cardinality labels.

failureModes.name: Churn from Ephemeral Batch / CI Jobs
failureModes.description: Pushgateway or short-lived serverless functions emit metrics with unique `execution_id` or `commit_sha` labels, creating permanent series churn that bloats the TSDB block index for 15–90 days.
failureModes.mitigation: Never include `execution_id` or `timestamp` in labels; emit batch outcomes as structured log events or aggregate via StatsD/OTel Delta temporality.

commonMistakes: Adding `user_id`, `email`, `ip_address`, `trace_id`, or `request_id` as a Prometheus/OTel metric attribute.
Logging raw HTTP paths (`/orders/12345`) or unparameterized SQL queries as metric labels instead of route templates (`/orders/:id`).
Creating a 20-bucket histogram with 5+ labels (`method`, `route`, `status`, `pod`, `az`, `tenant`) without calculating the Cartesian product.
Setting `sample_limit: 0` (unlimited) on Kubernetes service-discovery scrape configs, allowing any developer deploy to take down shared monitoring.
Using `labeldrop` in `metric_relabel_configs` without realizing it causes timestamp collisions instead of summing the dropped dimension.

sections.content:
## The idea

Time-Series Databases (TSDBs) like Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, and Mimir are optimized for **low-cardinality numerical aggregation** over time, not arbitrary relational indexing. Every unique combination of metric name and key-value labels (e.g., `http_requests_total{method="GET", route="/users/:id", status="200"}`) is assigned a unique internal **Series ID**.

While individual numerical samples compress remarkably well (~1.37 bytes per sample using Gorilla XOR and delta-of-delta encoding), the **inverted index** mapping every `label_name=label_value` pair to its list of Series IDs—plus the active **Head block** holding the last 2 hours of chunks—lives in RAM. Cardinality control is the discipline of keeping that Cartesian product bounded so memory, disk index size, and query fan-out stay predictable.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace how a single misconfigured metric is caught and neutralized before it can OOM-kill a shared Prometheus/Mimir cluster:

1. **Application emission:** An instrumented API emits `http_request_duration_seconds` with 12 `le` buckets, `route="/v1/orders/ord_99123"`, `user_id="u_4410"`, and `status="200"`. Across 50,000 active users in 2 hours, this produces `50,000 × 12 = 600,000` active series from one endpoint.
2. **OTel Collector / Scrape guardrail:** Before ingestion, the OTel Collector `attributesprocessor` (or Prometheus `relabel_configs`) inspects the metric. It strips `user_id`, normalizes `route` via regex/router template to `/v1/orders/:id`, and moves `trace_id` into an **Exemplar** attachment rather than a label.
3. **Quota enforcement:** Prometheus enforces `sample_limit: 25000` and `label_limit: 25` on the scrape job. If an unapproved metric still breaches the cap, the scrape fails with a `sample_limit exceeded` alert rather than poisoning the Head block.
4. **TSDB Head & Compaction:** The normalized metric creates just `12` series in the TSDB Head block (~48 KB RAM instead of ~2.4 GB). Every 2 hours, the Head block flushes cleanly to an immutable disk block and ships to S3/GCS via Thanos/Mimir.

sections.content:
## Designing cardinality budgets and alternatives

Treat metric cardinality like a finite memory budget across your organization:

- **Rule of thumb:** Keep any single metric under 10,000–50,000 active series, and keep `label_values` per label under 100 wherever possible.
- **Exemplars for high-cardinality context:** Instead of labeling `http_request_duration_seconds` with `tenant_id` or `order_id`, enable OpenMetrics Exemplars. Prometheus stores only the latest exemplar per series/bucket in a tiny ring buffer, linking latency outliers directly to Jaeger/Tempo traces.
- **Native Histograms:** Classic histograms multiply cardinality by `N` `le` buckets (typically 10–15). Prometheus Native Histograms pack exponential buckets into a single series, immediately cutting histogram cardinality by 90%.

## Choosing the right telemetry signal

| Signal Type | Storage Backend | Cardinality Tolerance | Typical Retention | Use For |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Metrics** | Prometheus / Mimir / VictoriaMetrics | Low (<100k series/metric) | 15d–13m (downsampled) | Alerting, SLO burn rates, dashboards, autoscaling |
| **Exemplars** | Prometheus OpenMetrics buffer | High (`trace_id` per bucket) | Hours–days | Jumping from p99 metric spike to a slow trace |
| **Structured Logs** | ClickHouse / Loki / Elasticsearch | High (`user_id`, `ip`, `url`) | 7d–90d | Audit trails, error payloads, ad-hoc user debugging |
| **Distributed Traces** | Tempo / Jaeger / Honeycomb | Unbounded (`request_id`) | 3d–14d (tail-sampled) | Cross-service latency waterfalls, N+1 DB queries |

## Failure modes

**1. Silent target drop from `sample_limit`:** Setting `sample_limit` protects Prometheus, but if nobody alerts on `up == 0` or `scrape_samples_post_metric_relabeling > limit`, a service loses all observability silently after a deploy.

**2. Label explosion from error messages:** Putting `error="connection refused to 10.0.4.18:5432"` in a metric label creates a new series for every transient IP/port/timeout string. Always map errors to a fixed enum (`error_type="db_timeout"`).

**3. Multi-tenant Mimir/Cortex ingestion rejection:** Shared TSDBs enforce `max_global_series_per_user` (e.g., 150,000). A single runaway team can hit the tenant cap and drop *all* production alerts for that tenant.

## Auditing cardinality in production

Use Prometheus's built-in TSDB status endpoints and PromQL diagnostics to catch leaks before they page you:

- **TSDB Top 10:** Query `/api/v1/status/tsdb` (or `topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))`) to rank metrics by active series count.
- **Churn rate:** Alert on `rate(prometheus_tsdb_head_series_created_total[15m])`—steady creation of thousands of new series per minute indicates ephemeral labels (`pod_uid`, `request_id`) leaking into metrics.
- **Head memory:** Track `prometheus_tsdb_head_series * 4096` as a quick lower bound on Head RAM requirements.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Enforce route template normalization (`/users/:id`, never `/users/12345`) in all HTTP/gRPC server middleware.
- [ ] Ban `user_id`, `session_id`, `ip`, `trace_id`, and raw exception strings from metric labels in code review and CI linters.
- [ ] Set `sample_limit` and `label_limit` on every Prometheus scrape job and `max_global_series_per_user` on multi-tenant remote-write.
- [ ] Replace 12+ bucket classic histograms with Native Histograms (or reduce buckets to 6–8 critical SLO thresholds).
- [ ] Alert on `up == 0` and `rate(prometheus_tsdb_head_series_created_total[15m])` spikes to catch cardinality regressions immediately after deploys.

interviewProblems.title: Metrics Cardinality Control
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Metrics Cardinality Control. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Metrics cardinality is the number of unique label-value combinations (`metric_name + {k=v}`) tracked in a Time-Series Database; unbounded labels like `user_id` or `request_id` explode inverted indexes, exhausting TSDB RAM and crashing Prometheus/Mimir.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Prometheus TSDB Head applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Compactor & Object Store.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Compactor & Object Store experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Set `sample_limit: 50000` and `label_limit: 30` per scrape job so rogue targets fail to scrape rather than crashing the central TSDB.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Never put high-cardinality identifiers (user IDs, IPs, URLs with UUIDs, pod hashes) into metric labels; keep active series bounded by dropping/normalizing labels at scrape time and use Logs or Trace Exemplars for per-request debugging.
Avoid trap: Adding `user_id`, `email`, `ip_address`, `trace_id`, or `request_id` as a Prometheus/OTel metric attribute.
Avoid trap: Logging raw HTTP paths (`/orders/12345`) or unparameterized SQL queries as metric labels instead of route templates (`/orders/:id`).
When to reach for it: Instrumenting multi-tenant or high-traffic microservices with Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, or Datadog where metrics aggregate across thousands of pods and endpoints.
When to reach for it: Enforcing guardrails at the OTel Collector or Prometheus scrape/remote-write layer before untrusted application metrics hit central TSDB storage.

putItTogether.title: Putting Metrics Cardinality Control Together
putItTogether.summary: Never put high-cardinality identifiers (user IDs, IPs, URLs with UUIDs, pod hashes) into metric labels; keep active series bounded by dropping/normalizing labels at scrape time and use Logs or Trace Exemplars for per-request debugging.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Metrics Cardinality Control before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Prometheus OOM-killed repeatedly during 2-hour head-block compaction. Adding a `metric_relabel_configs` rule to drop `uri` values not matching known patterns restored stability, followed by configuring Spring Boot's `WebMvcTagsProvider` to emit parameterized route templates.
